newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-SAMPRAS STARTS OPEN CAMPAIGN WISER BUT SADDER.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-SAMPRAS STARTS OPEN CAMPAIGN WISER BUT SADDER.

text.p: World number one Pete Sampras said the emotional strain of the past 12 months has forced him to re-evaluate his priorites as he prepares his challenge for the Australian Open title.
The U.S. Open champion last year lost his coach and mentor Tim Gullikson to a fatal brain tumour and split with his girlfriend of six years, Delaina Mulcahy.

"From a tennis point of view, 1996 was great. I finished number one again, and won the U.S. Open, so I have no complaints," Sampras told Melbourne's The Age newspaper in an interview published on Monday.
But events off the court forced the 25-year-old American to reassess his values outside the closeted world of professional tennis.
"Losing Tim, breaking up with my girlfriend after six years...I had to deal with things, real-life things that I never had to deal with before.
"As an athlete you kind of lose touch with things, at least I know I have. When things like this happen it just wakes you up a bit about life.
"Tennis is this great game....but it's not the most important thing in life. Being healthy and happy is.

"I've got the second half of my life to look forward to and I've thought about that a lot more than I once did since Tim passed away," said Sampras, who will begin his campaign in Melbourne against qualifier Dinu Pescariu of Romania on Tuesday.
His return to Melbourne Park will have added personal significance for Sampras, who is chasing his second Australian Open title after his triumph in 1994.
It was here two years ago that Gullikson was taken ill and hospitalised after suffering a relapse.
Sampras carried the torment over his friend's illness onto the centre court, sobbing uncontrollably near the end of his quarter-final against compatriot Jim Courier.
Despite the obvious emotional strain, Sampras rallied to beat the two-time Australian Open champion in five sets.
